title: The Address (Snapshots)
tagline: Marga Minco’s post-war return to a stranger’s house, and the objects she decides not to reclaim.

overview.intro: A woman returns to the street where her belongings were left during the war and finds that the address no longer belongs to anyone she knows. The story is built on objects — a silk dress, lace, silver — and on the refusal to take them back. The unit studies how a spare, delayed narrative carries historical catastrophe without describing it, how objects function as memory, and why the narrator walks away from the house and ends the story there.

learningOutcomes: Summarise what the narrator seeks and what she actually does.
Explain the significance of the objects the story names.
Account for the effect of the encounter at the door.
Analyse the story’s restraint in handling war and loss.
Answer extract and long questions on symbol and structure.

blocks.text: The story’s premise is a single journey made years after a catastrophe the text never describes. The narrator has an address — given to her during the war by the woman who was to keep her family’s things — and she walks to it with the intention of seeing her mother’s belongings again. The delay matters: because the narration is retrospective and quiet, the reader assembles the background from hints rather than from exposition, and the story’s method is established at once: nothing is explained, everything is implied.

As she approaches, the description is careful and sensory — the street, the bell, the waiting — because the journey is interior as much as geographical. She expects the address to return her past, and the story’s first irony is that she does not know what she wants: to see the objects, to have them, or simply to confirm that something survived. An examination answer should note that the story never settles which of the three it is until the final refusal, and that uncertainty is the point.

items: The war is never described; the reader infers it from the address.
The journey is years late and partly symbolic.
The narrator’s aim is ambiguous: sight, possession or confirmation.
The approach is rendered through sensory detail rather than explanation.
Suspense comes from what the house will contain.

learn.title: The woman at the door and the objects

blocks.text: At the door she meets a woman who does not know her, and the belongings are produced — or their presence is established — as ordinary household things. The encounter is the story’s hinge and its coldest moment: the narrator sees her mother’s silver, her lace, her dress in the hands of strangers, arranged as their own. The other woman’s manner is polite and possibly a little defensive, and there is no exchange that could settle the question of who the objects belong to, because ownership in the story has already been dissolved by the events that separated the narrator from them.

The objects are doing the heaviest work in the story. They are specific and domestic rather than valuable in the abstract — a dress, lace, cutlery — because such things carry a person: they were chosen, used and kept, and their reappearance in an alien kitchen is the war’s crime stated in miniature. The narrator’s reaction, moreover, is physical rather than argumentative: she recognises, hesitates, and does not demand. For examination purposes, the answer should always return to what the objects stand for — continuity of a family life that was interrupted — rather than to their material worth.

learn.title: The refusal, the nurse’s home and the ending

blocks.text: What the narrator finally does is the story’s meaning. She does not carry the objects away, and the story moves from the house to another place entirely — the nurse’s home or children’s home connected with the woman — where the separation between her and her past is completed. The refusal is not resignation: it is a recognition that taking the silver back would not restore what was lost, and that the objects, having lived another life for years, no longer belong only to her. The story’s title therefore points at two addresses at once — the street she walks to, and the place where her past actually is, unreachable.

The ending is deliberately abrupt, and its restraint is the technique. The narrator tells us what she did and stops; there is no meditation, no accusation, no scene of grief. The effect on the reader is stronger for it, because everything the story withheld — the war, the family, the years — rushes into the silence after the last sentence. Answers about the ending should say precisely this: that the story refuses emotional display in the same way the narrator refuses the objects, and the two refusals are one act.

items.text: Seeing her mother’s silver in a stranger’s kitchen.
items.note: The war’s displacement stated through one ordinary household scene.
Refusal as the only act that preserves what the loss destroyed.

blocks.text: Extract questions ask about the effect of a detail. Structure the answer: literal situation, the detail’s emotional or historical weight, and its place in the story’s movement. On the silver: it is her mother’s, it is in a stranger’s hand, therefore possession has passed but memory has not — and the narrator must choose between reclaiming the thing and keeping the meaning.

Long questions ask about objects as symbols or about the story’s treatment of war. In both, quote two named objects, explain what each carries, and show the sequence recognition → hesitation → refusal. Weak answers retell the visit; strong answers show how the story withholds exposition and lets objects do the historical work.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator find when she reaches the address?
questions.answer: She finds the house occupied by people who do not know her and have no idea who she is. The belongings her family had left — including her mother’s dress, lace and silver — are there, kept as part of the household’s ordinary things, and they are shown to her or seen by her in the strangers’ keeping. The woman at the door is polite but the meeting settles nothing: there is no explanation of how the objects came to be there and no ground on which ownership could be argued.
questions.explanation: The answer must include the unknown occupant and the objects in ordinary use.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator take nothing with her when she leaves?
questions.answer: She takes nothing because she recognises that the objects cannot give back what their loss represents: carrying the silver home would furnish a room but would not restore the family life that was interrupted by the war, and the things have lived for years in another household, so reclaiming them would be an act of possession rather than of recovery. The refusal is therefore active rather than defeated — it is the one choice left to her that keeps the meaning of the loss intact instead of reducing it to a dispute over goods. Her decision also mirrors the story’s method: just as she declines to make a scene at the door, the narration declines to explain or accuse, and both refusals leave the reader to feel what is not said.
questions.explanation: Three reasons are required: restoration is impossible, the objects’ meaning outweighs their ownership, and the refusal mirrors the narrative’s restraint.

questions.prompt: How does the story use objects to carry its meaning? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The story assigns to objects the work that exposition usually does, because it withholds the war entirely. The first object-cluster belongs to the narrator’s past: a silk dress, lace and silver cutlery, each naming a dimension of family life — the mother’s presence in how she dressed, the time invested in handmade lace, and the shared table at which occasions occurred. These are domestic rather than precious things on purpose, since their value is biographical and their reappearance among strangers therefore reads as displacement rather than as loss of property. The second object is the address itself, a piece of paper that becomes the narrator’s only remaining connection to her past and that organises the whole plot: she follows it, and following it is what forces the encounter. The third cluster is what the story withholds: the narrator recognises the objects, hesitates, and takes nothing, and that refusal converts the objects from evidence of a claim into evidence of a loss that no claim can repair. Structurally the objects also pace the story — anticipation on the journey, recognition at the door, renunciation on leaving — so that the emotional movement is carried by things rather than by statements, and the final silence after the last sentence is the emptiness where the objects would have been. For examination purposes the answer should quote at least two named objects, explain what each carries, and show that the story’s entire history of war and separation is delivered through them without once being narrated.
questions.explanation: Full marks require two or more objects explained for their meaning, the observation that the war is never described, and the sequence from anticipation to renunciation traced through the things.

questions.prompt: Is the story about recovering the past, or about accepting that it cannot be recovered? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case for recovery is built on the journey itself. The narrator keeps an address for years, returns to the street deliberately, and walks to a door with the intention of touching what remains of her family’s life — such persistence implies that the past is stored somewhere and can be reached. Her detailed sensory memory as she approaches, the precision with which she describes the setting, and the fact that she can identify her mother’s belongings on sight all suggest a past that has survived intact and is merely misplaced. The address, on this reading, is a key, and the story is the unlocking of it. The case for acceptance rests on what happens at the door. The woman does not know her; the objects have been absorbed into another household; no one can explain or contest how they came to be there; and the narrator, after recognising everything, makes no claim. The refusal to carry anything away is decisive: had the story wanted recovery, its climax would be the reclaiming of the silver, and instead the climax is the renunciation of it. The subsequent move to the children’s home completes the separation — her past has been distributed to places she can visit but never reassemble — and the abrupt ending, with no reflection and no accusation, performs the same acceptance in narrative form. The balanced judgement is that the story is about the attempt to recover and the discovery that recovery was never on offer: the journey is necessary so that the refusal can be genuine, because one cannot decline what one has not first sought. That also explains the title — the address is the object of the quest and the proof of its failure, since a door that leads to strangers cannot lead back to the past. The strongest answers will hold both halves: the persistence that motivates the return, and the renunciation that concludes it, showing that the story’s emotional force depends on the attempt being made rather than on its outcome.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings evidenced — the journey as recovery, the refusal as acceptance — and a judgement about how the attempt makes the renunciation meaningful.
